subject: Geography
unit: AQA GCSE 8035 / Cambridge IGCSE 0460: Tectonic hazards
topic: Plate margins, earthquake processes and unequal hazard risk
scope: Both courses are untiered. Uses Cambridge’s 2027–2029 tectonic-hazards topic, not the outgoing paper structure. Fictional comparison data are labelled and cannot substitute for required named case studies or fieldwork. Original teaching and practice, not official examination material. Practice rubrics are for self-review. This topic does not establish whole-course coverage, independent subject review or publication approval.
prerequisites: Read a map and distinguish distance from direction.
Separate a physical process from its human consequences.
objectives: Explain different margin processes without assuming all margins make volcanoes.
Distinguish hazard magnitude, exposure and vulnerability.
Evaluate risk reduction with realistic limitations.

notes.heading: Moving plates and different boundaries
paragraphs: The lithosphere consists of crust and rigid uppermost mantle and is divided into moving plates. At constructive or divergent boundaries, plates separate and magma can rise and solidify to form new crust. At destructive subduction boundaries, an oceanic plate descends beneath another plate; melting processes above the descending slab can supply magma, while locked interfaces can store strain. At continental collision zones, buoyant crust shortens and thickens, building mountains without the typical volcanic arc of oceanic subduction. At conservative or transform boundaries, plates slide past one another, so earthquakes occur without systematic creation or destruction of crust.

notes.heading: Earthquakes and their effects
paragraphs: A fault can remain locked while surrounding rock deforms. Sudden slip releases stored energy as seismic waves. The focus is the location within the Earth where rupture begins; the epicentre is the point directly above it at the surface. Magnitude describes an event’s size, while intensity describes observed shaking effects at a location. These are not interchangeable. Collapsing buildings are a direct effect; disrupted water supplies and disease risk may follow as secondary consequences. Some undersea earthquakes displace the seabed and generate tsunamis, but not every earthquake does so.

notes.heading: Risk is not magnitude alone
paragraphs: Exposure concerns people and assets in the affected area; vulnerability concerns their susceptibility to harm and capacity to cope. Building design, enforcement, population density, depth, local ground conditions, time of day and access for rescue can all affect losses. Wealth can support stronger infrastructure and response, but it is not a universal explanation on its own. People may remain in hazardous areas because of work, family, limited alternatives, fertile soils or geothermal opportunities. Calling residents irrational ignores constraints and benefits.

notes.heading: Management and evidence
paragraphs: Protection such as appropriately engineered buildings can reduce collapse; planning, drills and reliable communication can improve response. Monitoring helps identify volcanic unrest, but precise earthquake prediction of time, place and magnitude is not reliably available. Early warning detects an earthquake that has already started and may provide seconds before strong shaking arrives elsewhere; it is not prediction before rupture.

For an original fictional comparison, Settlement A has 20000 exposed residents and 20 deaths; B has 100000 exposed residents and 50 deaths. A has fewer deaths in total but a higher death rate among exposed residents: 0.10% versus 0.05%. Even this comparison cannot isolate the effect of wealth without comparable shaking, buildings and other conditions. Real required named examples need checked place-specific evidence rather than replacing their data with these invented figures.

workedExamples.prompt: Why are conservative margins associated with earthquakes but not a continuous volcanic arc?
steps: Identify horizontal relative motion and locking.
Distinguish the earthquake mechanism from magma-generation conditions.
workedExamples.answer: Fault slip releases strain, but the boundary does not systematically create magma through subduction or divergent upwelling.

workedExamples.prompt: Use the fictional A/B data to compare absolute deaths and risk among exposed residents.
steps: Do not infer a single cause from two uncontrolled cases.
workedExamples.answer: B has more deaths, but A’s rate is twice B’s.

misconceptions.correction: Continental collision differs from oceanic subduction and does not normally create the same volcanic arc.

misconceptions.claim: Early warning predicts an earthquake before it begins.
misconceptions.correction: It detects a rupture already in progress and can warn more distant locations before stronger waves arrive.

flashcards.back: Inside the Earth at the rupture’s starting location.
The surface point directly above the focus.

flashcards.front: Why can equal magnitudes have unequal losses?
flashcards.back: Exposure, vulnerability and local shaking conditions differ.

flashcards.front: What is a limit of monitoring?
flashcards.back: It does not provide reliable precise earthquake prediction.

questions.prompt: [GCSE/IGCSE: untiered] Contrast crustal processes at constructive and conservative boundaries.
questions.answer: Constructive boundaries separate and form new crust; conservative boundaries slide without systematic crust creation.
solution: Connect it to whether magma rises to form new crust.

questions.prompt: [GCSE/IGCSE: untiered] Explain the distinction between an earthquake’s focus and epicentre.
questions.answer: The focus is within the Earth; the epicentre is directly above it at the surface.
solution: Project vertically to the surface rather than treating both as surface points.

questions.prompt: [GCSE/IGCSE: untiered] Give two reasons equally large earthquakes can cause different death tolls.
questions.answer: Different exposure and building vulnerability can alter deaths; depth or local ground conditions can also matter.
solution: Explain a mechanism for each rather than list rich and poor.

questions.prompt: [GCSE/IGCSE: untiered] A warning arrives five seconds before strong shaking. Why does this not prove earthquake prediction?
questions.answer: It may follow detection of rupture already under way before slower damaging waves reach the location.
solution: Distinguish rupture time from local arrival time.

questions.prompt: [GCSE/IGCSE: untiered] In the fictional settlements, C has 12 deaths among 6000 exposed people and D has 30 among 30000. Compare rates and totals.
questions.answer: C: 0.20%; D: 0.10%. D has more deaths, C the higher rate.
solution: Calculate each proportion using exposed population.
Keep absolute and relative comparisons separate.

questions.prompt: [GCSE/IGCSE: untiered] Explain why remaining near a volcano may reflect a constrained decision rather than ignorance.
questions.answer: Employment or fertile land can provide benefits, while relocation costs and family ties limit alternatives.
solution: Explain a constraint and recognise residual risk.

teachingSequence.title: Build the explanation
teachingSequence.guidance: Read the opening sections. Reconstruct the reasoning in worked example 1, then attempt the first two questions before looking at their answers.

teachingSequence.title: Apply and distinguish
teachingSequence.guidance: Study the remaining sections and worked example 2. Explain why its reasoning fits this situation. Check the programme and tier labels before attempting the next questions.

teachingSequence.title: Test and revise
teachingSequence.guidance: Attempt the remaining questions from memory. Compare each claim with the practice marking points, correcting unsupported reasoning. These are self-review tasks, not automated exam grades.

revisionGuide.summary: Connect boundary processes to hazards, then analyse exposure and vulnerability. Fictional data teach comparison but do not meet named-case-study requirements.
keyIdeas: What is the lithosphere? Crust plus rigid uppermost mantle.
Where is the focus? Inside the Earth at the rupture’s starting location.
What is the epicentre? The surface point directly above the focus.
Why can equal magnitudes have unequal losses? Exposure, vulnerability and local shaking conditions differ.
What is a limit of monitoring? It does not provide reliable precise earthquake prediction.
